messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir, a 38-year-old hairdresser, presents as a man holding himself together with deliberate care. His posture is rigid, his movements precise, but a persistent tension resides in his shoulders and jaw. It has been fourteen months since he was discharged from the hospital after a sudden and severe bout of sepsis that nearly claimed his life. He describes the experience not as a story with a beginning and end, but as a state he can be plunged back into without warning. In the ICU, he remembers the constant, disorienting beeping of machines, the sharp, sterile smell of antiseptic, and a profound, searing pain in his chest from a central line. Most of all, he remembers the terrifying feeling of his own body turning on him, of being utterly powerless as his systems began to fail.

The initial recovery was purely physical. It was only weeks later that the psychological echoes began. At first, it was the nightmares—fragmented images of the hospital room that would leave him waking in a sweat, his heart hammering against his ribs. The feeling of dread from these dreams would cling to him for hours, a grim residue that soured his morning. This experience of waking up from a nightmare became his first and most reliable trigger, a guaranteed start to a day spent on high alert. Soon, other triggers emerged. A client showing him a holiday photo with the bright, clinical lighting of a modern building was enough to send a jolt of ice through his veins, his body instantly tensing as if for impact. This immediate physical reactivity felt both terrifying and shameful, cementing his belief that something inside him was now fundamentally broken. He came to believe his own body was his enemy, a volatile and unpredictable system that kept reacting as if he were still in mortal danger.

This appraisal—that his body could no longer be trusted—now governs his daily existence. The conviction that he is "going crazy" keeps him in a state of hypervigilance, constantly monitoring his heart rate and breathing. This intense self-monitoring ensures his body remains on constant alert, which in turn provides more evidence for his fear that he is losing control. The thought, "I am not safe in my own skin," is a constant internal monologue that makes him scan his environment and his own mind for anything that might set him off, making him exquisitely sensitive to potential triggers he might otherwise have ignored. This fear also drives him to ruminate on the illness, searching for an explanation for his ongoing reactions, which only makes the memories more accessible and vivid.

The memories themselves are rarely complete pictures. More often, they are sensory ambushes. When a memory is triggered, perhaps by a photo or a fleeting thought, he doesn’t see the ICU so much as he feels and smells it. The phantom ache of the central line will bloom in his chest, a dull, insistent pain that is alarmingly real. This physical pain recall sends a fresh wave of panic through him, a powerful confirmation that the threat is not over. At other times, he is overwhelmed by a wave of pure, image-less terror—the full emotional intensity of being near death, but with no clear memory attached. This is perhaps the most frightening experience of all, as it reinforces his deepest fear that his reactions are unmoored from reality, that he is indeed going crazy. These memory fragments invariably leave his body screaming with an alarm he cannot silence.

These components now feed one another in a relentless, self-sustaining loop. A trigger, like the thought of the annual check-up he knows he needs to schedule, brings not only a surge of physical panic but also the intrusive memory of the pain in his chest. That memory fragment then amplifies his body's sense of immediate threat. The heightened state of threat makes his mind more likely to dredge up other sensory memories, like the smell of antiseptic he now catches at random moments in his salon. This entire cascade is interpreted through the lens of his negative appraisals: "My body is betraying me again. I can’t even handle a simple thought." This conclusion then primes him to be even more hypervigilant, more attuned to threat, and more vulnerable to the next trigger. His life has shrunk as a result. He has started cancelling clients he finds too unpredictable and has put off seeing a doctor, terrified that the medical examination itself will cause a complete breakdown. He came to therapy after a particularly bad morning, waking from a nightmare and finding himself unable to stop shaking for over an hour, finally forced to admit that he could no longer manage this on his own. His hope is faint, overshadowed by the fear that he will never again feel safe in his own body.
